nameStory: The 'bloody' in bloody crane's-bill refers to the deep magenta-red color of its vibrant flowers, which can appear almost blood-red in bright sunlight. The 'crane's-bill' part comes from the long, pointed seed pods that look remarkably like a crane's beak stretching skyward. When the seeds are ripe, these 'beaks' split open with a satisfying pop, flinging seeds in all directions!
description: Bloody crane's-bill is a low-growing, spreading perennial wildflower that forms dense mats of deeply divided, palm-shaped leaves. It produces striking magenta-pink flowers about an inch across throughout much of the growing season. The plant typically grows 8-12 inches tall but can spread 12-18 inches wide, creating attractive groundcover patches. Its sturdy stems and compact growth make it a hardy, reliable bloomer in gardens and wild spaces alike.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright magenta-pink flowers with five rounded petals and darker veins running through them. Each flower is about an inch across with ten prominent stamens creating a fuzzy center. The petals feel silky-smooth to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply cut, palm-shaped leaves divided into 5-7 narrow, finger-like segments that feel slightly fuzzy and have a fresh, green scent when crushed. Leaves turn beautiful orange-red in fall.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, pointed seed pods that really do look like crane beaks, standing upright about an inch tall. When ripe, they split with an audible 'pop' and curl back dramatically to fling seeds away.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mounds that hug the ground, with stems that branch outward from the center. The plant feels sturdy and substantial when you brush against it, not delicate like some wildflowers.

habitat: Look for bloody crane's-bill in rocky areas, dry slopes, and well-drained soils throughout New England, often in partial shade or woodland edges. It thrives in sandy or gravelly soils and can be found growing among other rock garden plants and drought-tolerant wildflowers. While not extremely common, it's occasionally found naturalized from gardens or growing in disturbed areas with good drainage.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small rosettes of deeply divided leaves, with first flowers appearing in late spring. The fresh green foliage has a clean, pleasant scent.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with continuous magenta-pink flowers from early summer through late summer. Seed pods develop and pop open regularly during hot, dry days.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn stunning shades of orange and red, making the plant decorative even without flowers. Late flowers may still appear in warm weather.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level in harsh winters, but in milder areas some basal leaves may persist, appearing bronze or reddish.

funFact: The seed pods don't just split open—they literally explode! On hot, dry days you can actually hear the 'pop' as the pods burst and watch the seeds shoot up to 10 feet away, making this one of nature's most entertaining seed-dispersal mechanisms.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with wild geranium, but bloody crane's-bill has much more deeply divided leaves (cut nearly to the base) and more intensely colored magenta flowers, while wild geranium has less divided leaves and paler pink-purple blooms. Memory trick: 'bloody' flowers are more intensely red-colored than other crane's-bills.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse these true geraniums with the common garden 'geraniums' sold at nurseries—those are actually pelargoniums from South Africa. True geraniums like bloody crane's-bill are hardy perennials that can survive New England winters, while garden 'geraniums' are tender and need to be brought indoors.
compareHints: Among New England's crane's-bills, bloody crane's-bill stands out for its deeply divided leaves that are cut almost to the base, creating very narrow segments. Wild geranium has much broader leaf divisions, while Herb Robert has more finely divided, fern-like leaves and tiny pink flowers. The intense magenta color of bloody crane's-bill's flowers is also more vivid than most of its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild geranium stands out from its cranesbill cousins by its substantial size, soft pink flowers, and preference for rich woodlands.
Among New England's wild geraniums, Herb Robert is the most delicate and lacy-looking, with much more finely divided leaves than the larger Wild Geranium.
Among New England's crane's-bills, rock crane's-bill is unique for its low, mat-forming growth and intensely fragrant leaves - most others grow more upright and have much less scented foliage.
Northern cranesbill is much smaller and more delicate than wild geranium, with tiny lavender flowers instead of large pink ones.
Thunberg's Geranium is much smaller and more delicate than our common Wild Geranium, with more finely divided leaves and smaller flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Carolina crane's-bill has the smallest flowers - much tinier than the showy inch-wide blooms of wild geranium or the medium-sized flowers of Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, meadow crane's-bill is one of the largest and most robust, forming much bigger clumps than most relatives.

Among New England's crane's-bills, dusky crane's-bill is unique for its nearly black flowers with backward-curved petals - our native wild geranium has pink flowers that face upward, while Herb Robert has small bright pink flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, dove's-foot stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety leaf texture and low, mat-forming growth habit.
Among New England's crane's-bills, this is one of the tiniest and most easily overlooked.
Purple-vein geranium stands out from other New England geraniums primarily by its bright blue flowers - most other species have pink, white, or purple blooms.

Among New England's crane's-bills, cut-leaved crane's-bill stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - while wild geranium has broader, less deeply cut leaves and Herb Robert has more triangular leaf segments, cut-leaved crane's-bill looks almost feathery.
Among New England's crane's-bills, little-robin is the tiniest - much smaller than wild geranium or Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Long-stalked stands out for its exceptionally long flower stalks and deeply dissected leaves.

Richardson's geranium differs from New England's common wild geranium by having paler flowers with more prominent dark veining, perfectly straight (not curved) seed beaks, and more finely divided leaf segments.
Wood crane's-bill differs from our native wild geranium by having more deeply dissected leaves and typically stronger purple coloring with more prominent petal veining.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Siberian Crane's-bill would be one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
